units.text: The lights died at nine and the whole street went dark with them, and now a single candle gutters on the formica table while Sam Holloway, who has not slept properly since the summer of 1974, pours two fingers of rye into a chipped mug, and Jules, Sam's partner at the precinct, leans against the humming, silent fridge with a flashlight pointed at the floor and a cigarette burning down between two nicotine-stained fingers.
Rule one of a blackout. Nobody trusts anybody. Not even the guy who drove you here.
units.name: SAM

units.text: They cut the phone lines before the power. That's not weather, Sam.
units.name: JULES

units.text: I knew the day I took the badge that every kitchen in this city would end up like this one. Quiet. Waiting for the other shoe.
units.name: SAM

units.text: They're across the street. I counted two. Maybe three.
units.name: JULES

units.text: They have a way of looking at the window. Same way my father looked at it. Like it owed him money.
units.name: SAM

units.text: A car idles somewhere outside, headlights sweeping the curtains once, twice, and moving on.
So we sit here and drink?
units.name: JULES

units.text: The truth about waiting is that it never ends. It just changes clothes.
units.name: SAM
